title: FetchError conflates a TLS validation failure with a network failure
description:
## What

pkix_mta_sts_http::FetchError::Transport(String) carries both:

  - the policy host's certificate did not validate
  - the connection was refused, reset, or never established

as one opaque string, because ureq and reqwest report them as incompatible types and the variant was written to erase that difference.

## Why it matters

The HTTPS certificate is an MTA-STS policy's ONLY authentication. The _mta-sts TXT record is unsigned; the policy body carries no signature. So "the certificate did not validate" means "this policy may have been written by an attacker", and "the connection was refused" means "the domain's web server is down". Those are not the same event and a sender should not treat them alike.

Two concrete consequences:

TLSRPT CANNOT REPORT IT. RFC 8460 §4.3.2.2 defines sts-webpki-invalid as "the MTA-STS Policy could not be authenticated using PKIX validation" -- the most security-relevant thing a report can say about MTA-STS. pkix-tlsrpt cannot produce it, because classifying Transport that way would tell a domain its certificate is broken whenever its policy host is merely down, sending an operator after a certificate that is fine. There is a test in pkix-tlsrpt asserting no FetchError maps to sts-webpki-invalid, so this gap is pinned rather than forgotten.

AN OPERATOR CANNOT ALERT ON IT. §3.3 asks senders to "alert administrators (through the use of logs or similar) when such attempts fail". A deployment that wants to page on "someone may be MITM-ing our policy fetches" but not on "example.com's web server is down" cannot write that rule today.

## What to do

Add a variant -- TlsValidation(String), or similar -- and populate it from each backend:

  ureq     ureq::Error::Io wrapping a rustls error. Needs checking what
           ureq 3 actually surfaces; it may require inspecting the io error's
           source chain for a rustls::Error, which is fragile but at least
           localised to one place.
  reqwest  reqwest::Error has no is_tls(), but the error source chain
           reaches rustls::Error. Same approach.

Both are string- or downcast-matching on a dependency's internals, which is why this was not done inline: it wants a deliberate decision about how fragile a classification is acceptable, and a test per backend that a bad certificate produces the new variant.

If neither backend can distinguish it reliably, that is also an answer -- but then the Transport documentation should say so explicitly, rather than leaving a reader to assume the distinction is available.

## Testing it needs a bad certificate

Which is why this is not trivial: the existing destination-policy tests work because mta-sts.localhost resolves to loopback and is refused before any TLS. Testing a certificate failure needs a TLS listener presenting a certificate that does not validate -- a self-signed cert on a local port, or a known-bad public endpoint such as expired.badssl.com (network-dependent, so #[ignore]d like the resolver's live tests).

## Acceptance

[ ] Decide whether each backend can distinguish a TLS failure reliably, and record the finding
[ ] If yes: a FetchError variant for it, populated from both backends
[ ] A test per backend that a certificate that does not validate yields it, not Transport
[ ] pkix-tlsrpt's classify_fetch_error maps it to sts-webpki-invalid, and the test asserting the gap is updated to assert the mapping instead
[ ] If no: FetchError::Transport's documentation states that the distinction is unavailable and why
